chapters.title: Chapter 5: Funding Gaps, Tax Outflows and Surplus Cash

lessons.title: The Tax Calendar and Your Cash: GST, TDS and Advance Tax Outflows

children.text: Customers negotiate. Suppliers can be asked for time. The tax calendar does neither. It is a set of fixed dates that remove real money from your bank account whether or not anyone has paid you, and for most Indian businesses it is the single most predictable and least planned-for outflow of the year. This lesson maps those dates, shows how much cash they take, and explains why two of the three biggest ones are not really your money at all.

body.text: GST and TDS are collected by you on somebody else's behalf. That money passes through your account, it does not belong to it, and spending it is the most expensive short-term loan available anywhere in India.

children.text: Three Different Kinds of Tax Cash

body.title: Money you owe, and money you are merely holding

columns.label: Your own tax
points: Advance tax and self-assessment tax on your profits
Paid from money the business has actually earned
Amount depends on how profitable the year is
Instalments on 15 June, 15 September, 15 December and 15 March

columns.label: Tax you collect for the government
points: GST charged on your invoices, net of input credit
TDS deducted from salaries, contractors, professionals and rent
Never yours, even for a day
Due on fixed monthly dates regardless of your cash position

body.text: The second column is where businesses get into serious trouble. Using collected GST or deducted TDS to fund a shortfall feels harmless because the money is sitting in the account. It carries interest, penalties, disallowance of the related expense and, for TDS, potential prosecution in serious cases. No supplier and no bank will ever charge you what the tax department does.

children.text: The Month, as Your Bank Account Experiences It
Here is a typical month for Konkan Ceramics, with ₹1 crore of monthly sales and ₹70 lakh of purchases. GST figures assume an 18% rate on both sides, purely to show the mechanism.

events.title: TDS deposited: about ₹2 lakh
events.description: Tax deducted last month from salaries, job work, professional fees and rent. For March deductions the due date runs to 30 April.

events.title: GSTR-1 filed
events.description: Outward supplies return. No cash moves, but your buyers cannot claim their input credit until this is filed, so it directly affects when they pay you.

events.title: PF and ESI paid: about ₹3 lakh
events.description: Employer and employee contributions for last month. The employee share, like TDS, is money you are holding for someone else.

events.title: Advance tax instalment
events.description: On 15 June, 15 September, 15 December and 15 March, based on estimated profit for the whole year.

events.title: GSTR-3B filed and GST paid: about ₹5.4 lakh
events.description: Output tax of ₹18 lakh less input credit of ₹12.6 lakh. Quarterly filers under QRMP follow a different schedule, with monthly payment challans.

stats.label: Statutory outflow, ordinary month
stats.context: TDS ₹2 lakh, PF and ESI ₹3 lakh, GST ₹5.4 lakh

stats.label: September, with advance tax
stats.context: The same month as the festive build-up

stats.label: Annual GST paid in cash
stats.context: Net of input credit, on ₹12 crore of sales

children.text: Notice the collision. September carries the largest statutory outflow of the half-year and the heaviest festive stock build-up at the same time, which is exactly why the bridge in Lesson 4.1 showed ₹38 lakh leaving the bank in a month budgeted to earn ₹10 lakh of profit.
Advance Tax: Paying on Profit You Have Not Collected
Advance tax is due on the profit you expect to earn for the year, in four instalments, on cumulative percentages. Konkan Ceramics expects ₹1.2 crore of profit and around ₹30 lakh of tax.

body.caption: Advance tax schedule on ₹30 lakh of estimated annual tax

body.text: Advance tax is charged on profit earned, not cash collected. A business whose receivables have ballooned still pays tax on those invoices, which is why a bad collections year and a large advance tax payment tend to arrive together. Forecast the instalments from your budget, as in Lesson 4.1, and treat them as immovable.

body.title: How much by December?
body.prompt: A company estimates its total tax for the year at ₹30 lakh. By 15 December, what cumulative amount of advance tax should it have paid, in ₹ lakh?
body.explanation: The cumulative requirement by 15 December is 75%, so ₹22.5 lakh. Having paid ₹13.5 lakh by September, the December instalment is ₹9 lakh. Shortfalls attract interest under Section 425 of the Income-tax Act, 2025, which carried over from Section 234C of the Income-tax Act, 1961, with further interest under Section 424, formerly Section 234B, where the total paid falls short of 90% of the assessed tax.

children.text: GST: Where the Cash Actually Leaks
GST is designed to be neutral, since you collect it and pass it on. In practice it has three specific cash effects that every manager should recognise.
Tax is due on the invoice, not the collection.
For a supply of goods, liability generally arises when the invoice is issued, so the tax on April sales is paid in May while the customer pays in July.
Input credit depends on your supplier's behaviour.
Credit is available only when the supplier has reported the invoice and it appears in your auto-populated statement. A supplier who files late holds up your credit and your cash.
Credit and cash are separate ledgers.

Input credit sits in the electronic credit ledger and can only be used against output tax. If your credit builds up faster than your liability, that is real cash locked with the government until a refund is claimed, which is common for exporters and for inverted duty structures.

body.title: The 180-day rule that turns a payables decision into a tax cost

children.text: Under the second proviso to Section 16(2) of the CGST Act, 2017, read with Rule 37 of the CGST Rules, a buyer who claims input credit but does not pay the supplier the invoice value plus tax within 180 days of the invoice date must add that credit back to output tax liability, with interest. The credit can be reclaimed when payment is eventually made.
Put that next to Lesson 3.2 and the picture is complete. Stretching a supplier past 180 days now costs you three things at once.
The input credit reverses,
so cash leaves through the GST return.
Interest applies
on the reversed amount.
For a micro or small supplier,
the MSMED interest and the deferral of the deduction under Section 37(2)(g) of the Income-tax Act, 2025, formerly Section 43B(h) of the Income-tax Act, 1961, apply long before day 180.
This rule has been the subject of amendment discussion, so confirm the current position and timelines with your chartered accountant before relying on the detail.

body.title: Whose money is it?
body.question: Cash is short. Which of these amounts sitting in your bank account is genuinely the company's own money to use?
options: GST collected on last month's invoices, net of input credit
TDS deducted from contractor payments last week
The employee share of provident fund deducted from salaries
The balance left after all of the above, representing collected profit
body.explanation: The first three are collected or deducted on behalf of someone else and are merely passing through. Only what remains after setting them aside belongs to the business. Companies that treat the gross bank balance as available working capital are, without realising it, funding operations with trust money.

body.title: The monthly deadline
body.textWithBlank: TDS deducted during a month must generally be deposited by the ___ of the following month.
body.explanation: The 7th, with deductions for March allowed until 30 April. Late deposit attracts interest of 1.5% per month or part of a month, and because part months count in full, being one day late typically costs two months of interest.

body.text: Do the arithmetic on that. Deposit ₹2 lakh of TDS on the 8th instead of the 7th and interest runs for the month of deduction and the month of payment, two part months, at 1.5% each. That is ₹6,000 for one day, an annualised cost in the thousands of percent, plus the late filing fee on the quarterly return that follows.

body.title: The 20th, and the money is not there
body.scenario: It is the 18th. GST of ₹5.4 lakh is due on the 20th, PF was paid on the 15th, and the forecast shows ₹6 lakh in the bank. A dealer has promised ₹12 lakh but his accounts team says the payment run is on the 27th. The sales head suggests filing the return and paying the GST a week late, arguing that "everybody does it and the interest is small".
body.prompt: What do you actually do between now and the 20th?
body.modelAnswer:
Treat it as a two-day cash problem, not a compliance choice.
1. First, confirm the exact number. Recheck the input credit available in the auto-populated statement, since a supplier filing late may be the reason the liability looks higher than expected. Sometimes the shortfall is smaller than the first estimate.
2. Work the collections list for 48 hours, not the whole book. Call the three largest customers with invoices already approved, and ask specifically for a same-day transfer, not a promise.
3. Check the cash credit headroom and drawing power from Lesson 5.1. This is precisely what a revolving limit exists for: a two-day timing gap against money arriving on the 27th.
4. If there is no headroom, discount one accepted invoice. The cost of discounting ₹30 lakh for 45 days was about ₹35,000 in Lesson 5.1, and a two-day bridge is a fraction of that.
5. Move controllable outflows out of the 19th and 20th: a vendor payment on agreed terms with room to spare, a non-urgent purchase, any advance payment.
Why not simply pay late.
6. Interest applies on delayed GST payment, and late filing carries a fee per day. Worse, the return history is visible: your buyers can see your filing status, and a pattern of late filing affects their input credit and their willingness to give you terms.
7. It also affects borrowing. Banks routinely compare GST returns against reported turnover at renewal, and irregular filing raises questions you do not want to answer in Lesson 5.1's meeting.
Afterwards, fix the structure.
8. Set up a separate sweep or sub-account and move GST, TDS and PF into it as they are collected, so the 20th is funded on the 1st.
9. Put the statutory calendar into the 13-week forecast permanently, as fixed rows that nobody may edit.
10. Tell the sales head plainly: "everybody does it" is not an argument, and a two-day gap has at least four legitimate solutions that cost less than the interest.

body.title: Put the tax calendar into your cash planning
steps: List every statutory payment your business makes, with its due date and typical amount.
Add them as fixed, non-negotiable rows in the 13-week forecast from Lesson 4.2.
Estimate advance tax from the budgeted profit and diarise all four instalment dates at the start of the year.
Open a separate account or sweep, and move GST, TDS and PF amounts into it as they are collected or deducted.
Reconcile input credit monthly and chase suppliers who file late, because their delay is your cash.
If you export or face an inverted duty structure, track the credit balance building up and file refund claims promptly.
Check ageing payables against the 180-day input credit rule before the quarter closes.
Review with your chartered accountant once a year whether the timing of any payment or filing can legitimately be improved.

cards.definition: Your own tax on estimated annual profit, paid in four instalments on 15 June, September, December and March.
Tax deducted from payments you make and deposited by the 7th of the following month. Never your money.
Where GST input credit sits. Usable only against output tax, not withdrawable as cash.
Money actually deposited with the GST system to settle liability that credit cannot cover.
The consolidated TDS framework effective 1 April 2026, replacing the scattered provisions of the 1961 Act.
Input credit reverses if a supplier is not paid within 180 days of the invoice, and is reclaimed on payment.

points: The tax calendar is the most predictable outflow in the business and the least planned: TDS on the 7th, PF and ESI on the 15th, GST on the 20th.
GST and TDS are collected on behalf of others. Only what is left after setting them aside is genuinely the company's cash.
Advance tax is charged on profit earned, not cash collected, so a bad collections year still produces a large September instalment.
Konkan Ceramics pays about ₹10.4 lakh of statutory dues in an ordinary month and about ₹19.4 lakh in September, during its heaviest stock build-up.
GST is due on the invoice while the customer pays later, and input credit depends on suppliers filing on time.
Being one day late with ₹2 lakh of TDS costs about ₹6,000, because part months count in full. Fund statutory dates first, always.

body.text: Konkan Ceramics is fictional. GST rates, the 25% tax rate and all amounts here are illustrative, not current rates for any product or taxpayer. Due dates, thresholds and the provisions summarised, including the 180-day input credit rule and the transition to the Income-tax Act, 2025, can change and depend on your filing category. Confirm the current position with your chartered accountant. This is not tax advice.
